events.question: I get migraines.
events.answer:
Migraine is a recurring neurological condition. Its most common feature is headache, often with nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light and sound. Most people have episodes, and a minority have chronic migraine. (Source: *Migraine*, general clinical reference)

A typical attack is often one-sided and pulsating, and it can get worse with routine physical activity. Untreated attacks commonly last from several hours to three days. (Source: *Migraine*, general clinical reference)

One point guidance stresses is medication-overuse headache. Frequent use of acute headache medicines can keep headaches going and turn an episodic pattern into a chronic one. The guidance gives monthly limits on treatment days, and it says this overuse is common and reversible. If you take headache medicine often, raise this with a clinician. (Source: *Migraine: acute treatment, when prevention starts, and medication-overuse limits*, national headache society guidance)

Some headache patterns need urgent care rather than a routine appointment. These include a sudden, severe headache that peaks within a minute, a headache with fever and a stiff neck, a headache with new neurological symptoms, or a headache after a head injury. If you have any of these, seek emergency care now. (Source: *Migraine: acute treatment…*, which points to separate emergency guidance for these)

The sources I searched don't cover treatment choices, doses, or prevention options, so I can't advise on those. A clinician or headache specialist can discuss them with you.

What would you like to know more about, such as how migraines are typically described, when to see a clinician, or how medication overuse works?

events.question: About eight a month at the moment.
events.answer:
Thanks for sharing that. About eight attacks a month is a useful detail to take to a clinician. I can't tell from this alone what pattern you have.

The *Migraine* general clinical reference says chronic migraine is defined as headache on 15 or more days a month, with at least eight of those having migraine features, lasting over three months. Eight attacks a month is below that line, but the reference says the definition depends on how many headache days you have, not only on attacks, so counting all your headache days may matter.

The *Migraine: acute treatment, when prevention starts, and medication-overuse limits* guidance also sets limits on how often acute medicines are used. It says to keep treatment days under ten a month for triptans, ergots, opioids and combination pain relievers, and under fifteen a month for simple pain relievers. If you take any headache medicine on many of your attack days, that is worth raising with a clinician, because the guidance says overuse is common and reversible.

The sources I searched don't say which medicines suit you or whether your pattern calls for a change in treatment. A doctor or headache specialist can review your headache diary and medicine use with you.

Could you tell me roughly how many days a month you have any headache, and whether you take medicine for them on many of those days?

events.question: They usually start on the right side.
events.answer:
Migraine headaches are classically one-sided, so a right-sided pattern fits the typical description. The *Migraine* general clinical reference also says the headache is bilateral (both sides) in a substantial proportion of people, so side alone does not tell you whether migraine is the cause. A clinician would look at the whole pattern.

Some features need emergency care, not a routine appointment. The *Sudden neurological symptoms that may indicate a stroke* guidance says to call emergency services immediately for sudden severe headache with no known cause, or for sudden face drooping, arm or leg weakness or numbness, slurred speech, confusion, vision loss, or trouble walking. If any of these happen with your headaches, get emergency care now.

The sources I searched don't describe how to tell migraine from other headache types by location alone. A clinician can review your headache diary, including which side and how often, and decide what needs checking. (Note: my first search returned material on coding systems and joint conditions, which was not relevant, so I used the *Migraine* reference for this answer.)

Could you tell me whether the headaches on your right side ever come with the symptoms listed above, or whether the pattern has changed recently?

events.question: Light and noise make them worse.
events.answer:
Sensitivity to light and sound is a common feature of migraine attacks. The *Migraine* general clinical reference lists sensitivity to light and sound among the usual features, alongside nausea and vomiting. (Source: *Migraine*, general clinical reference)

Light sensitivity can also be a warning sign in other conditions. The *Signs suggesting meningitis or meningococcal infection* guidance says to call emergency services immediately if severe dislike of bright light comes with headache and fever. It also lists fever with a severe headache and a stiff neck, and a rash of small red or purple spots that does not fade when pressed. If you have any of these, get emergency care now.

The sources I searched don't cover ways to manage light or noise sensitivity, or treatment options. A clinician can discuss those with you.

Has the light sensitivity ever come with a fever, a stiff neck, or a rash?

events.question: I take ibuprofen when one starts.
events.answer:
Ibuprofen is one of the medicines the migraine guidance discusses. The *Migraine: acute treatment, when prevention starts, and medication-overuse limits* guidance says that using acute headache medicine too often can keep headaches going. It sets the limit for simple pain relievers at fewer than fifteen treatment days a month. The sources I searched don't name ibuprofen, so I can't confirm which limit applies to it. A pharmacist or clinician can check that. If you take it on most of your roughly eight attack days, or on other headache days too, that is worth raising with a clinician. The guidance says this kind of overuse is common and reversible.

The osteoarthritis guidance I found says oral anti-inflammatory painkillers, a group that includes ibuprofen, carry stomach, heart and kidney risks that should be assessed first. That guidance is about a different condition, so it is only a general point. It is a good reason to ask a clinician or pharmacist about your own use.

My search also returned unrelated material on asthma, diabetes, anxiety and thyroid care, which I did not use.

Could you tell me roughly how many days a month you take ibuprofen, including any days you take it without a full attack?

events.question: Is that the right thing to be taking?
events.answer:
I can't tell you whether ibuprofen is the right choice for you. The sources I searched don't say which medicine suits a particular person, so a clinician or pharmacist needs to decide that with you.

The *Migraine: acute treatment, when prevention starts, and medication-overuse limits* guidance does say that a medicine is usually judged over two or three separate attacks before deciding it doesn't work, because attacks vary a lot from one to the next. It doesn't name ibuprofen or say whether it fits your situation.

The same guidance says preventive treatment is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling enough that acute treatment alone isn't enough. It describes the threshold as four or more migraine days a month with some disability. Your roughly eight attacks a month could meet that threshold, depending on how much the attacks disrupt your daily life. That is a useful question to bring to a clinician.

To prepare for that appointment, you could note how often you take ibuprofen, how well each attack responds, and how much each attack affects work, sleep, or daily activities.

Could you tell me whether your attacks stop you from doing your usual activities, or whether you mostly manage them and carry on?

events.question: And at eight a month, would prevention be considered?
events.answer:
The guidance I found says preventive treatment is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling enough that acute treatment alone isn't enough. It sets the threshold at four or more migraine days a month with some disability, or fewer attacks when disability is severe. (Source: *Migraine: acute treatment, when prevention starts, and medication-overuse limits*, national headache society guidance)

At about eight attacks a month, you would be above the four-day frequency mark. Whether prevention is offered would depend on how much the attacks disrupt your life. The guidance also says the aim of preventive treatment is to reduce how often and how severely you get attacks, not to stop them altogether. It describes a 50 percent reduction in migraine days as the usual sign that a treatment is working. (Source: same guidance)

The sources I searched don't say which preventive treatments exist or which would suit you, so I can't advise on that. A clinician can judge whether prevention fits your situation.

My search also returned unrelated material on heart disease and cholesterol, which I did not use.

Could you tell me how many days a month you have any headache, not only full attacks? That would help a clinician judge how often you are affected.
